where: Section 2, round rule bullet ('After each round, a process keeps the value that appears in a majority...')
problem: The rule is undefined when no value has a strict majority, and that case really occurs. With N = 2f+1 and f crashes a process can receive exactly two values, one 1 and one 0 (for example N = 3, f = 1, one process crashed, the two survivors propose different values). The student has no instruction for this tie, so the described algorithm is incomplete.
fix: State the complete rule: each process counts its own current value plus every value it received, and adopts the value with a strict majority; if two values are tied, it adopts the smaller of the two. Add: 'Without a firm tie-break rule the algorithm is not defined, because ties do occur whenever a crashed process leaves the survivors split.'

problem: The bullets mix two different algorithms. 'Every process sends the set of values it knows' describes flooding/relaying of sets, which is agreed by taking the minimum, while 'keeps the value that appears in a majority' describes single-value majority voting, where each process sends only its current value and never a set. A student cannot tell which one to implement, and counting a majority over sets is not well defined.
fix: Keep one algorithm: 'In each round every process sends its single current value to every other process; after the round it replaces its value by the majority among its own value and the values received (ties broken toward the smaller value).'

where: Section 2, opening paragraph and 'Why f+1 rounds?'
problem: The round-based majority algorithm is presented without saying that it needs the synchronous model. The rounds only terminate, and a crashed process's silence only counts as a missing value, if message delay and process speed are bounded. Section 4 mentions this, but a reader of Section 2 alone will think the algorithm works in any timing model.
fix: Add one sentence at the start of Section 2: 'This algorithm assumes the synchronous model: a bound on message delay lets each round finish in known time, and a process that sends nothing within that time is counted as crashed.'
